advances: The sharp target at the actual central centroid for the integer-reflected common-vertex planar triangle family of any length. Symmetric pairs are taken around an occupied center.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Only through-point caps need be checked, since tightening any containing halfspace parallel to itself decreases its mass. A pure base through-cap has mass $V(1+\sum_{j>0}r_j^2)=V(M+1)/2$. For the other directions use 6f616779219fd76c at base zero, with the touching affine majorant $r_j\le1$; ignore zero-area fibers in its positive-radius hypotheses. Its replacement is one actual cap, no larger on any fiber. Interchanging the two coordinates if needed reduces to $a x_1+(1-a)x_2+\beta j\ge t$, with $t=1/3$, $1/2\le a\le1$, and arbitrary real $\beta$.

For $m=0$ or if the two endpoints of the $m=1$ chain have zero area, ordinary triangle depth at the centroid is $4V/9$ by d6ce3858d2712450, and an apex cap attains it (in the sole positive-area fiber). For $m=1$ with $r_1>0$, use 1a7377b8dcb5b16b. Translate the prototype to centroid zero and put back each actual fiber centroid as the translation of its scaled prototype. The midpoint inclusion follows from $r_1\le1$. Each endpoint has area strictly below $VM/2$, so whether the middle is heavy or all fibers are nonheavy, that fact selects the actual middle centroid. For the all-normal conclusion it remains to treat $m\ge2$; the sector formulas below hold for every $m$ unless specified.

Write $F_{a,r}(u)$ for cap mass divided by $V$ in $rT$ at threshold $u$. For $r>0$ and $1/2<a<1$, the normalized vertex heights are $0,d_0,1$ with $d_0=(1-a)/a$. At $x=u/(ar)$, the dimensionless tail $F_{a,r}(u)/r^2$ is $1-x^2/d_0$ on $[0,d_0]$, $(1-x)^2/(1-d_0)$ on $[d_0,1]$, and respectively one and zero outside those two intervals. These are the similar-triangle formulas in the proof of d6ce3858d2712450. The case $r=0$ has zero area. A reflected pair at distance $h>0$ has cost $F_{a,r_h}(t-h|\beta|)+F_{a,r_h}(t+h|\beta|)$.

The fixed-height minimum over a nonnegative pair shift follows from the same accepted fact's two-tail calculation. For $q=t/(ar)\ge1$ the minimum is zero at shift zero. For $q<1$ the candidates in units of $r^2$ are the zero-shift value, the full/empty cost one, and the straddling value $1-(2q-1)^2/(2d_0-1)$ if $d_0>1/2$ and $1/2\le q\le d_0$. A flat straddling case at $d_0=q=1/2$ has value one. This classification exhausts the minima by differentiability of the clipped tail for distinct vertex heights. If $a\ge2/3$, then $q\ge d_0$, $d_0\le1/2$, and the zero-shift value is at most one: it is largest at $r=1$, where $2(a-1/3)^2\le a(2a-1)$. Thus the minimum is at zero shift for each pair. At $a=1$ this comparison follows by continuity of every cap area at fixed tilt, since the boundary is a line and the height range is nonzero. Consequently all the pairs attain their floors at the one common tilt zero, and
$$
\frac{\inf_\beta \operatorname{cap}(a,\beta)}V
=\frac{a}{2a-1}\sum_j(r_j-1/(3a))_+^2.
$$
The chosen-peak truncation of facc699f7957afd2 applies with peak value 1 at index m in the full sequence of length 2m+1, including zero endpoints, and exponent two. In particular $\sum_j(r_j-c)_+^2\ge(1-c)^3 M+c(1-c)^2/(2m+1)$ for $0\le c\le1$, since its $\kappa_0(0)\ge1/(2m+1)$. For $c=1/(3a)$, the factor $a(1-1/(3a))^3/(2a-1)$ is at least $1/4$: it is $1/4$ at $2/3$, and its derivative is $(3a-1)^2(3a-2)/[27a^3(2a-1)^2]\ge0$. The positive finite correction makes this sector's bound strict above $VM/4$.

For $1/2<a<2/3$, take $c,\rho,A,L,B,k,\lambda,E$ as in the finite quadrature lemma. Now $d_0>1/2$, and $q\ge1/(3a)>1/2$ for all $r\le1$. If $r\le c$ the pair minimum is zero. If $c<r\le\rho$, then $q\ge d_0$, so the zero-shift cost is at most $2(1-d_0)<1$ in units of $r^2$ and minimizes. For $r\ge\rho$ the straddling value is at most one and is no larger than the zero-shift cost, since their difference multiplied by $d_0(2d_0-1)$ is $2(d_0-q)^2$. In the three radius regimes the resulting costs are $0$, $2A(r-c)^2$, and $r^2-(2/3-ar)^2/[a(2-3a)]$, respectively. These equal $2k(r)$, with equality of branch values at $c,\rho$.

The own fiber pays $F_{a,1}(t)=1-1/[9a(1-a)]=k(1)+g$, where $k(1)=2/3-1/(9a)$ and $g=(2-3a)/[9(1-a)]>0$. Thus every original common tilt pays at least $g+\sum_j k(r_j)$ in units of $V$. This uses separate pair floors only as lower bounds. For $r\le1$ the inequality
$$
(r-\rho)_+\le\frac{1-\rho}{1-c}(r-c)_+
$$
gives $k(r)\ge a(6a-1)(r-c)_+^2/(3a-1)^2$. The same accepted truncation gives $\operatorname{cap}(a,\beta)/V\ge g+vM$, where $v=(3a-1)(6a-1)/(27a^2)$. Its excess over $2/9$ has numerator $12a^2-9a+1$ over $27a^2$, so this already proves the bound for $\alpha\le a<2/3$, where $\alpha=(9+\sqrt{33})/24$.

For $m\ge2$ and $1/2<a<\alpha$, a cap strictly below $2VM/9$ would require $M>M_0=9/2-1/[2a(1-a)]$ by the own fiber, and $M>M_1=g/(2/9-v)$ by the second budget. Concavity and $m\ge2$ give $r_1\ge(1+b)/2$ and $r_2\ge b$, hence $M\ge1+2((1+b)/2)^2+2b^2=M_2(b)$. The quadrature lemma and first budget give
$$
\operatorname{cap}(a,\beta)/V-2M/9
\ge g+(\lambda-2/9)M+k(b)-\lambda[b^2+(1-b)^2/3]-2BE(b).
$$
The coefficient of $M$ is positive. Replace $M$ by $\max(M_0,M_1,M_2(b))$ and apply aea5b6d88072013c, with its actual domain $1/2<a<\alpha$, $0\le b\le1$, to make the right side nonnegative. Its $k,E$ branches agree at the stated joins and $b=1$ uses the finite first branch of $E$. This contradicts the assumed bad cap.

Finally, at $a=1/2$, $F_{1/2,r}(u)$ is the clipped tail $r^2-4u^2$ on $0\le u\le r/2$. The pair minimum is $8t(r-2t)_+$. For $r\le2t$ zero shift gives zero. Otherwise both thresholds remain in the proper interval until the upper threshold hits $r/2$ at shift $r/2-t\le t/2$; the sum decreases up to that point and subsequently the sole remaining tail increases to its full value. Evaluating at the support hit gives the stated minimum. The own cap is $5/9$.

For the needed finite hinge correction when $m\ge1$, set $f(v)=6(v-2/3)_+-v^2$. Its integral on $[0,1]$ is zero, and it can change sign only from negative to positive (it is negative up to $2/3$, and increasing from there). Its upper-tail integrals and $f(1)$ are nonnegative. The inverse-radius step density and plateau argument of the quadrature lemma now gives $\int_0^m f(r(z))\,dz\ge0$. The hinge term is convex and the negative square contributes error $-\delta_i^2/6$ per cell, so
$$
\sum_j f(r_j)\ge f(b)-\sum_i\delta_i^2/3\ge f(b)-(1-b)^2/3\ge-13/27 .
$$
The last minimum is at $b=2/3$, by concavity on $[0,2/3]$ and increase on $[2/3,1]$. Thus $\sum_j(r_j-2/3)_+\ge M/6-13/162$. Keeping the exact own cap and the pair floors gives
$$
\operatorname{cap}(1/2,\beta)/V
\ge 1/9+(4/3)\sum_j(r_j-2/3)_+
\ge 2M/9+1/243.
$$
All area statements use the actual integer samples. A common continuous dilation multiplies both sides by its squared factor.

statement:
Let $m\ge0$, $1=r_0\ge r_1\ge\cdots\ge r_m\ge0$, with nondecreasing outward drops $r_j-r_{j+1}$, and set $r_{-j}=r_j$, $b=r_m$, and $M=\sum_{j=-m}^{m}r_j^2$.

Let $T=\operatorname{conv}(0,e_1,e_2)$, $V=|T|=1/2$. At the consecutive integer bases $-m,\ldots,m$ take the actual fibers $r_jT$, and assume there are no other positive-area integer fibers. With the sum of ordinary areas on the fibers as measure, every closed ambient halfspace containing the actual point $(0,1/3,1/3)$ has mass at least $2VM/9$. For $m=0$ its exact depth is $4V/9$.

In the normalized coordinates, for $2/3\le a\le1$ and every $m\ge0$, the infimum over $\beta\in\mathbb R$ of the cap mass at $a x_1+(1-a)x_2+\beta j\ge1/3$, divided by $V$, is attained at $\beta=0$ and equals $[a/(2a-1)]\sum_j(r_j-c)_+^2$, $c=1/(3a)$. Each such cap has mass divided by $V$ at least
$$
\frac{a(1-c)^3}{2a-1}M+\frac{a}{2a-1}\frac{c(1-c)^2}{2m+1}>\frac M4.
$$
A common continuous dilation replaces $1=r_0$ by any $R>0$, the mark by $(0,R/3,R/3)$, and $M$ by the sum of the resulting squared radii.
